title: How the U.S. Can Survive a Large-Scale AI Cyberattack
gist: A CSIS commentary argues that frontier AI models with autonomous hacking capability (citing Anthropic's withheld Claude Mythos, scored at a 73 percent success rate on expert hacking tasks) put multi-sector attacks on U.S. critical infrastructure within reach of terrorist groups and individuals, not just states. Its remedy set is institutional rather than technical: a physical Cyber Unified Coordination Group operations center, a more authoritative CISA, expanded JCDC, and federally funded zero-cost threat-intel sharing plus defensive AI models built by the private sector.

themes.theme: Frontier AI Shifts the Offensive Cyber Threshold

insights.claim: Anthropic declined to publicly release its newest frontier model, Claude Mythos, because of its advanced hacking and vulnerability-detection capabilities, after the AI Security Institute measured a 73 percent success rate on expert hacking tasks in capture-the-flag simulations.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A named, quantified capability benchmark for offensive cyber AI — a leading indicator for demand in cyber-defense budgets and for model-release policy risk at frontier labs.
insights.quote: Mythos achieved an impressive 73 percent success rate in executing expert hacking tasks during capture-the-flag simulations.
insights.locator: While the above scenario may sound far-fetched

insights.claim: AI capability diffusion means future large-scale cyberattacks on critical infrastructure may be launched not only by nation-states but by terrorist organizations and individual actors, collapsing the attribution and deterrence logic built around state adversaries.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: If the attacker set widens beyond states, deterrence-by-retaliation degrades and spend shifts toward resilience and detection — favoring defensive cyber vendors over policy-based mitigation.
insights.quote: Future large-scale cyberattacks, with the help of AI, may not only be conducted by nation-state actors, but potentially now from terrorist organizations and individual actors as well.
insights.locator: While the above scenario may sound far-fetched

insights.claim: An AI-enabled cyberattack across multiple sectors is expected to create a degraded digital communications environment, which is precisely the condition under which a coordination body dependent on digital channels fails.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Degraded-comms assumptions drive procurement of resilient/out-of-band communications and physical continuity-of-operations facilities.
insights.locator: An AI-enabled cyberattack across multiple sectors

insights.claim: CISA is designated national coordinator for civilian domestic cybersecurity but lacks clear authoritative power to direct other U.S. government entities during a crisis, creating a command-and-control gap in any multi-department response.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Authority reform at CISA is the single highest-leverage legislative watch item for anyone modeling U.S. incident-response speed after a major attack.
insights.quote: While CISA is the national coordinator, it lacks clear authoritative powers to direct other government entities during times of crisis.
insights.locator: One way the U.S. government intends to synchronize itself

insights.claim: The Cyber Unified Coordination Group exists only as an informal multi-agency coordination forum that stands up upon a national cyber emergency, with no standing physical operations center.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Informal-only coordination is a structural fragility; a move to a standing facility would be a concrete budget line to track.
insights.locator: One way the U.S. government intends to synchronize itself

insights.claim: The proposed fix is a physical Cyber UCG operations center staffed by CISA, the Department of Energy, the FBI, the U.S. military, the intelligence community and state, local, territorial and tribal offices, on the argument that in-person communication is required for timely cross-organization coordination.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A specific, fundable policy ask — watch for it in FY appropriations and CISA reauthorization language.
insights.locator: To mitigate this, the U.S. government should plan

insights.claim: The Joint Cyber Defense Collaborative, run by CISA, is judged insufficient for a sizable cyber emergency because recent U.S. performance managing even smaller-scale incidents showed weaknesses in interagency coordination and centralized leadership.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Signals that observed small-incident response is a valid proxy for large-incident readiness — a bearish read on current U.S. resilience.
insights.locator: The Joint Cyber Defense Collaborative (JCDC), currently run by CISA

themes.theme: Electricity as the Single Point of Failure

insights.claim: U.S. power generation and transmission runs through over 7,000 continental power plants across three independent interconnection grids, and telecommunications, financial, healthcare and transportation sectors all depend on it absent long-term backup generation.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Grid dependency makes utilities and grid-security vendors the chokepoint asset in any AI-cyber scenario; backup generation and microgrid capex is the derivative trade.
insights.locator: The Department of Energy (DOE), for example

insights.claim: Coordination between CISA and the Department of Energy is framed as the load-bearing interagency relationship for keeping the other 15 U.S. critical infrastructure sectors functional during a cyber emergency.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Watch DOE-CISA joint exercises and information-sharing agreements as the practical readiness metric, not headline cyber budgets.
insights.locator: CISA and the DOE will need to be in lockstep

themes.theme: Private Sector Ownership and the Trust Deficit

insights.claim: The private sector owns and operates most U.S. critical infrastructure and, outside a few cases of federal regulation, contractual obligation and national emergency powers, is not required to cooperate with the government at all.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Voluntary-only cooperation means national cyber resilience is a corporate capex decision — regulatory mandates are the tail risk for infrastructure owners.
insights.locator: The private sector owns and operates most critical infrastructure

insights.claim: The author invokes Reagan's line about government help to argue the federal government has an image problem with industry that must be fixed before a major incident, not during one.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Trust — not authority or technology — is named as the binding constraint on incident response; new funding and information cross-sharing programs are the proposed currency.
insights.quote: “I’m from the government, and I’m here to help,”
insights.locator: The Private Sector Has a Shared Responsibility

insights.claim: CISA's biennial Cyber Storm exercise is presented as the mechanism for surfacing national deficiencies by running the most likely and most dangerous scenarios with critical infrastructure stakeholders.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Exercise participation lists are a cheap public signal of which firms are inside the national-security cyber perimeter.
insights.locator: Additionally, the government should continue to solicit participation

insights.claim: Anthropic's Mythos identified numerous vulnerabilities in internet browsers and operating systems but Anthropic chose not to publicly release most of that information, leaving other critical networks exposed even as the finding capability exists.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Proprietary vulnerability hoarding by frontier labs is a new systemic-risk channel and a likely target for disclosure regulation.
insights.quote: but Anthropic chose not to publicly release most of that information

insights.claim: Anthropic's Project Glasswing offered $100 million in credits to over 150 companies and the U.S. government to test Mythos so they can find and patch vulnerabilities before the model is eventually released.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A concrete template for pre-release defensive credit programs — the author argues this should become standard practice and be government co-funded, which would create a new procurement category.
insights.locator: While Anthropic has not released Mythos’ detected vulnerabilities

insights.claim: The prescription is that the private sector build defensively minded AI models that rapidly detect, remediate and share anomalies, malware and indicators of compromise, matching the scaling of offensive frontier capability.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Defensive AI security tooling is the named growth category if offensive frontier capability keeps scaling.
insights.locator: With the advent of frontier AI models that can scale offensive cyber

insights.claim: Existing cyber threat intelligence repositories such as LevelBlue OTX, MISP and VirusTotal are not all free or easily accessible, which prices smaller private organizations out of current threat information under competing budget constraints.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The paywalled-CTI gap is where federal subsidy is most likely to land, reshaping the commercial threat-intel market.
insights.locator: CTI repositories are another critical aspect

insights.claim: Information Sharing and Analysis Centers have been hit by funding cuts and now require membership fees in some cases, while the Automated Indicator Sharing program remains free, and a Congressional Research Service report found these programs had variable effect on private sector participation and value.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Evidence that existing federal sharing programs underdeliver — an argument for either reform funding or continued reliance on commercial vendors.
insights.locator: The U.S. government has attempted to find ways

insights.claim: The defensive logic is that raising the cost of infiltrating many critical networks at scale is what prevents an adversary from generating the simultaneous effects that constitute a major cyberattack.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Reframes cyber defense as denying simultaneity rather than preventing all breaches — a useful lens for judging which security spend actually reduces systemic risk.
insights.quote: The harder it is for an adversary or its AI systems to infiltrate multiple critical networks at scale, the harder it is going to be for them to generate simultaneous malicious effects that constitute a major cyberattack.
insights.locator: Regardless, the federal government should prioritize funding
